1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Trades the dark-squared bishops now that Black's bishop attacks the one on g5, and leaves the e5 pawn cramping Black. White keeps the space advantage and builds a broad pawn centre; Black has a solid but passive position and plays for a counter-strike against the centre.

A pawn gambit: the h-pawn protects the bishop on g5, so if Black trades, the h-file opens for a kingside attack on a king that struggles to find a safe place. Black's natural ...c5 break runs into a knight jump to b5. Sharp and risky, with an attack instead of a space advantage.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.background: A gambit devised by Adolf Albin and played by Chatard, it was not taken seriously until Alekhine's game against Fahrni at Mannheim in 1914.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Recaptures with the queen and keeps the right to castle; a king recapture would give it up for no reason. Black has given up the dark-squared bishop, so the cramped position needs a pawn break to free it, while White has the space.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Classical Variation
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.background: It used to be the main line of the French Defence, but the Burn Variation has since overtaken 4...Be7 in popularity, and 6.h4 now rivals 6.Bxe7 in frequency.

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Accepts the gambit: after the bishops are traded, Black's queen takes the g5 pawn and Black is a pawn up. The price is time and king safety, because White's pieces swing to the kingside while Black's king has no safe home.

Declines the pawn and takes the b5 square from White's knight, so the c-pawn can advance without that jump as an answer. White can keep the initiative with the queen to g4, threatening to take on e7 and then on g7, which forces Black to take on g5 and open the h-file. A wild game with unsafe kings.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Maróczy Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Strikes at d4 in the way Black normally meets this structure, but here it is too slow: the bishops come off and a knight lands on b5, threatening a fork on c7 and a check on d6. Black has to spend time on that, with the king under pressure from the advanced h-pawn.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Breyer Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Castles at once, but into the attack: the h-pawn is already advanced, and White's queen and bishops can aim at the kingside before Black has any counterplay. Playable, but risky; it is the king position the gambit was built to attack.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Spielmann Variation

1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.strategy: Strikes at the e5 pawn at once, but opens the e8-h5 diagonal: White's queen checks on h5 and the king has little cover. Black gets rid of the cramping pawn at the price of king safety.
1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5.name: French Defence: Alekhine-Chatard Attack, Teichmann Variation
